analysis.one_liner: Cuts the tax rate on large inherited estates from 40% to 20%.
analysis.headline: The bill to halve the top estate tax rate never got a hearing or a vote; it had no cosponsors and died in committee when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut the top rate on the estate tax — the tax on very large inheritances — from 40% to 20%, and would apply the cut retroactively to deaths and gifts after the end of 2019. It also exempts the cost of the cut from pay-as-you-go rules, which are the budget rules requiring that tax cuts or spending increases be paid for. The bill was referred to two committees, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs of the largest estates. The estate tax only applies after large exemptions, so the cut would go almost entirely to families with multi-million-dollar estates. Cutting the top rate from 40% to 20% roughly halves the tax on the portion of an estate above the exemption, and making it retroactive to January 1, 2020 would benefit estates of people who had already died when the bill was introduced.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the top rate on estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes from 40% to a flat 20% [S2][S3].
Applies the lower rate retroactively to deaths, gifts, and generation-skipping transfers occurring after December 31, 2019 [S3].
Exempts the revenue cost of the cut from statutory PAYGO rules and the Senate PAYGO scorecard, so it does not have to be offset by other tax increases or spending cuts under those rules [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Every dollar of estate tax not collected adds to deficits that are eventually financed by all taxpayers, while the direct benefit goes to a small number of the wealthiest households.
analysis.who_pays_short: All federal taxpayers, via added deficits

drawbacks.text: The cut would cut revenue roughly in half on the largest transfers, with the benefit concentrated on a small number of very wealthy families and the cost spread across all taxpayers through higher deficits [S2][S3].
The bill waives the pay-as-you-go rules that normally require tax cuts to be paid for, meaning the cost would not be offset under those rules [S2][S3].
A retroactive effective date raises fairness concerns for estates already settled under the 40% rate, and retrospective rate cuts are difficult for planners and courts to administer [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to heirs of the largest estates, roughly halving their tax on amounts above the exemption; the cost is lost federal revenue borne by everyone. Because the estate tax already exempts the vast majority of estates, the bill's effects on ordinary working people are almost entirely indirect — through the deficit — while its direct effect is a large transfer to wealthy families. Waiving PAYGO makes clear the cut was not designed to be paid for.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Budget committees, no hearing or vote was ever scheduled, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jodey Arrington introduced the bill on January 17, 2020, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Budget Committee [S1][S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off because the bill died: the estate tax remained at its current-law rate, and the revenue it raises was not cut. The families of large estates who would have benefited did not get the reduction.

for.name: Rep. Jodey C. Arrington
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the top estate tax rate to 20% and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat for the rest of the Congress and expired.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so there was no measurable partisan split — a single Republican sponsor and no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates (wealthiest households)
industries.note: A cut from 40% to 20% roughly halves the tax on large inheritances, with the benefit going almost entirely to families with multi-million-dollar estates. The cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory services
industries.note: A lower estate tax rate slightly reduces demand for avoidance planning, but cheaper transfers of large wealth generally expand the pool of family wealth those firms manage. The effect is modest either way.
